stories.head: Astrobotic's quick fix for lunar ambitions
stories.body: Astrobotic has been acquired by Voyager Technologies, a move aimed at scaling up for NASA’s lunar base initiative. The details of the deal remain undisclosed, but it suggests that sometimes a corporate merger is a stopgap for growth rather than a strategic overhaul. With NASA's Artemis program ramping up, Astrobotic's ability to deliver payloads could be a game changer.
stories.soWhat: If mergers were actually effective strategies, we’d see fewer companies scrambling for funding.

stories.head: Jio's LEO plans raise eyebrows ahead of IPO
stories.body: Jio Platforms is gearing up for an IPO while unveiling plans for a sovereign LEO constellation. This ambitious project is set against the backdrop of notoriously unpredictable satellite launches, which might make investors a bit queasy. The IPO is expected to attract significant attention, but the execution risk could be a deal-breaker.
stories.soWhat: Investors love the shiny new tech, but they might want to check the launch schedule first.

stories.head: True Anomaly raises $190M for co-orbital security
stories.body: True Anomaly secured $190 million in Series C funding, bringing its valuation to $1.6 billion. This round underscores the growing demand for co-orbital security and space domain awareness as defense priorities shift. With the DoD's increasing focus on space, True Anomaly is well-positioned to capitalize on this trend.
stories.soWhat: In space, cash often trumps actual innovation, and this funding round is proof.

talent.statLabel: Job orders YoY · plus 2 starters per head, an 8-year first
talent.head: Demand has doubled. So has our hit rate.
talent.body: EVONA's job orders are up 2.0× year-over-year, and for the first time in our eight-year history we're placing two new starters per EVONA staff member. The first number says demand is real. The second says we're converting it, which in recruitment is the only number that actually matters. Growth is heaviest in Series B/C startups; primes are running flat. Compensation isn't the variable. The constraint is schedule risk in the primes: senior engineers leave Boeing, Lockheed, Northrop because they want to ship hardware before retirement.
